A connection in I.23, not identity of all uses of gold and giving.

In III.14 Zarathustra reports his soul’s questions: who should give thanks, is giving a need and is receiving pity? These are the soul’s embedded questions rather than a settled definition of every gift.

In “The Great Longing” Zarathustra reports his soul’s questions: who should give thanks, is giving a need and is receiving pity? These are the soul’s embedded questions rather than a settled definition of every gift.

I.23 names the highest virtue as bestowing. In IV.01 Zarathustra calls the “honey sacrifice” a verbal ruse, spends what he has received and casts his happiness as bait into the human world. Giving is set beside deliberate attraction; the people’s response is not shown.

“The Bestowing Virtue” names the highest virtue as bestowing. In “The Honey Sacrifice” Zarathustra calls the “honey sacrifice” a verbal ruse, spends what he has received and casts his happiness as bait into the human world. Giving is set beside deliberate attraction; the people’s response is not shown.
The shepherd hears “bite”, bites off the snake’s head, spits it out and rises transformed, laughing; in III.13 Zarathustra describes his own illness through the same actions.
The shepherd hears “bite”, bites off the snake’s head, spits it out and rises transformed, laughing; in “The Convalescent” Zarathustra describes his own illness through the same actions.

In I.23 Zarathustra requires the disciples to leave separately, lose him and find themselves. A return is promised after they have denied him; friendship and a shared hope are named as a future expectation.

In “The Bestowing Virtue” Zarathustra requires the disciples to leave separately, lose him and find themselves. A return is promised after they have denied him; friendship and a shared hope are named as a future expectation.
The compound Krämer-Golde in an address to brothers; it is not simply a repetition of the image in I.23.
The compound Krämer-Golde in an address to brothers; it is not simply a repetition of the image in “The Bestowing Virtue”.
This comparison in I.23 rests on gold’s rarity, uselessness, mild radiance and continual self-giving. Other uses of gold in the book require separate reading.
This comparison in “The Bestowing Virtue” rests on gold’s rarity, uselessness, mild radiance and continual self-giving. Other uses of gold in the book require separate reading.

In III.04 blessing is named as a sky over each thing: chance, innocence and freedom from subjection to purpose. Here it concerns things; its object differs from the request to the sun and the relation between giver and receiver.

In “Before Sunrise” blessing is named as a sky over each thing: chance, innocence and freedom from subjection to purpose. Here it concerns things; its object differs from the request to the sun and the relation between giver and receiver.

“The Vision and the Enigma” objects to the ease of the answer; the passage does not state that Zarathustra rejects the formula altogether.

In IV.01 Zarathustra renames the honey sacrifice himself: the word was a verbal ruse, he spends what was given, and honey and his own happiness serve as bait for people. The comparison keeps a strategy of attraction beside the image of giving.

In “The Honey Sacrifice” Zarathustra renames the honey sacrifice himself: the word was a verbal ruse, he spends what was given, and honey and his own happiness serve as bait for people. The comparison keeps a strategy of attraction beside the image of giving.

In I.01 Zarathustra needs outstretched hands to give away his excess of wisdom. In I.23 he requires the disciples to leave him and find themselves. The comparison places two of his addresses to others together: a need for receivers and a demand for independent departure.

In “Zarathustra’s Prologue” Zarathustra needs outstretched hands to give away his excess of wisdom. In “The Bestowing Virtue” he requires the disciples to leave him and find themselves. The comparison places two of his addresses to others together: a need for receivers and a demand for independent departure.

In II.09 the giver seeks contact with the receivers’ souls and suffers the gulf between them. In III.04 blessing concerns things: Zarathustra restores chance to them and frees them from bondage to purpose. No receiver’s reply is shown here; the object of giving shifts from a relation between people to the freedom of things from purpose.

In “The Night-Song” the giver seeks contact with the receivers’ souls and suffers the gulf between them. In “Before Sunrise” blessing concerns things: Zarathustra restores chance to them and frees them from bondage to purpose. No receiver’s reply is shown here; the object of giving shifts from a relation between people to the freedom of things from purpose.
III.13 establishes the sequence of the summoned thought, the cry and the fall; no additional causation is asserted.
“The Convalescent” establishes the sequence of the summoned thought, the cry and the fall; no additional causation is asserted.

In I.23 Zarathustra himself requires the disciples to leave him. In II.09 it is the giver who suffers distance: others receive, yet he doubts whether he touches their souls and speaks of weariness from excess. The comparison sets a desired departure from the teacher beside the painful gulf between giving and receiving.

In “The Bestowing Virtue” Zarathustra himself requires the disciples to leave him. In “The Night-Song” it is the giver who suffers distance: others receive, yet he doubts whether he touches their souls and speaks of weariness from excess. The comparison sets a desired departure from the teacher beside the painful gulf between giving and receiving.

In I.01 the receivers bless the sun for its excess. In III.14 the soul asks whether, conversely, the giver should thank the receiver. The comparison turns on the direction of gratitude; the soul’s question remains a question.

In “Zarathustra’s Prologue” the receivers bless the sun for its excess. In “The Great Longing” the soul asks whether, conversely, the giver should thank the receiver. The comparison turns on the direction of gratitude; the soul’s question remains a question.
The comparison is made in I.23; it does not define every use of gold in the book.
The comparison is made in “The Bestowing Virtue”; it does not define every use of gold in the book.

In “The Great Longing” “I gave you everything” is followed by the clarification that telling the soul to sing was his last act; the text does not name it a separate “last gift”.
In II.09 Zarathustra asks whether he still touches the souls of those who take; in III.14 he reports his soul’s questions about giving as need and taking as pity.
In “The Night-Song” Zarathustra asks whether he still touches the souls of those who take; in “The Great Longing” he reports his soul’s questions about giving as need and taking as pity.

Zarathustra asks the sailors in “The Vision and the Enigma”; “The Convalescent” continues the question through the throat, bite and spitting in the teacher’s own recovery.
III.02 and III.13 permit a comparison of scenes, but the earlier wording could be read as identifying the figures.
“The Vision and the Enigma” and “The Convalescent” permit a comparison of scenes, but the earlier wording could be read as identifying the figures.

In III.04 Zarathustra restores chance to things and frees them from subjection to purpose. In IV.01 spending what he is given has an explicit aim: happiness is cast as bait for people. The comparison distinguishes things’ freedom from purpose from the deliberate use of a received gift to attract people.

In “Before Sunrise” Zarathustra restores chance to things and frees them from subjection to purpose. In “The Honey Sacrifice” spending what he is given has an explicit aim: happiness is cast as bait for people. The comparison distinguishes things’ freedom from purpose from the deliberate use of a received gift to attract people.
In IV.08 “Da lerntest du” is Zarathustra addressing the beggar; recht geben and recht nehmen are compared, and gut schenken is separately named an art.
In “The Voluntary Beggar” “Da lerntest du” is Zarathustra addressing the beggar; recht geben and recht nehmen are compared, and gut schenken is separately named an art.

In I.23 the teacher’s gift does not fix dependence: he requires the disciples to leave, reject him and find themselves. This is a concrete demand addressed to these listeners, available for comparison with receiving a gift.

In “The Bestowing Virtue” the teacher’s gift does not fix dependence: he requires the disciples to leave, reject him and find themselves. This is a concrete demand addressed to these listeners, available for comparison with receiving a gift.
In II.20 Zarathustra stops at this question; III.12 repeats redemption’s task, while in III.13 the animals unfold the recurrence of an entire life.
In “Redemption” Zarathustra stops at this question; “Old and New Tables” repeats redemption’s task, while in “The Convalescent” the animals unfold the recurrence of an entire life.
In the question of willing backwards and overcoming revenge against time. The speech in II.20 leaves this question open.
